claims.text: The target materials are nanoscale high-entropy alloys containing multiple principal elements.
Increasing alloy complexity introduces lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion introduced through alloy complexity improves high-temperature structural stability.
Lattice distortion introduced through alloy complexity improves high-temperature chemical stability.
Lattice distortion causes high self-interstitial atom migration energy.
Lattice distortion causes non-directional displacement-cascade propagation.
High self-interstitial migration energy and non-directional cascade propagation confine radiation-induced defects to a limited region.
Spatial confinement of defects increases defect recombination.
The proposed defect behavior improves radiation-damage tolerance.
Improved radiation-damage tolerance produces improved structural stability in high-temperature nanoalloys.
Improved radiation-damage tolerance produces improved chemical stability in high-temperature nanoalloys.
The distorted nanoalloy will be more structurally stable than an otherwise comparable high-entropy nanoalloy without lattice distortion.
The distorted nanoalloy will be more chemically stable than an otherwise comparable high-entropy nanoalloy without lattice distortion.
The proposed benefit should hold under high-temperature conditions below the alloy's melting point.
The magnitude or existence of the proposed stability benefit may depend on alloy composition and processing conditions.
Failure of the lattice-distorted material to show improved structural and chemical stability relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
